immerse

/ih-MURS/ - rhymes with rehearse · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Immerse means to involve oneself deeply and completely in something.

Before writing a note of the score, the composer immersed herself in Appalachian fiddle tunes, listening to little else for an entire winter.

Example

Assigned the harbor dispute, the new reporter immersed himself in it: he rode the dawn ferries, ate lunch with the dockworkers, sat through every council hearing, and read forty years of port records. Within a month, veterans on the beat were checking their facts with him.

Immerse literally means to dip completely underwater, and the figurative sense keeps that completeness: you don't just study the subject, you surround yourself with it until nothing else filters in.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

engross: Engross describes the grip a fascinating thing gets on you - the book engrosses its reader, pulling attention in whether or not she planned to give it. Immerse is what you do on purpose: choosing to surround yourself with a subject until nothing else filters in.

absorb: Absorb, like engross, is said of the thing that soaks up your attention - the crossword absorbed him for an hour. Absorption happens to you. Immerse runs the other way: the person deliberately plunges in and arranges life so the subject surrounds them completely.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

dabble: to try something casually, on the surface

skim: to touch only the surface, quickly

Where it sits · how completely the subject takes over

sample → engage → immerse

sample vs. immerse: Sampling a subject means one taste - a lecture here, a chapter there; immerse means diving in until the subject surrounds you.

engage vs. immerse: Engaging with a topic means giving it real attention; immerse goes further - shutting everything else out until the topic becomes your whole environment.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — im-: in, into

Root — merse: to dip, to plunge

Put it together: Im- (in, into) + merse (to dip, to plunge) = to plunge in. Latin mergere, 'to dip,' fathered a small family of plunging words in English - merge, emerge, submerge - and immerse is the member that plunges all the way in, first in water, then in work, languages, and hobbies.

Use the root in a new word: submerge: The submarine can submerge in under a minute once the dive alarm sounds.

Word Choice

neutral

Immerse is for total, surrounding involvement - the opposite of dabbling. Engross describes the pull a gripping book or task exerts on you; immerse describes what you do on purpose. Reach for it when someone chooses to live inside a subject for a while.
